name: vork
description: Headless 3D and VFX engine for agents. Research preview.
readmeExcerpt: vork, the Voyager rendering kernel, is a headless 3D and VFX engine built for agents. [Watch the film](https://voyager.so/vork): a car drives into the night as the forest turns into glowing cyan wireframe, drawn from real triangle edges by a scene shader. Credit: [“Car Concept”](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF-Sample-Assets/tree/main/Models/CarConcept) by Unity Fan, glTF adaptation by Eric Chadwick / Darmstadt Graphics Group, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: scaled, animated, brighter head and tail lights, wheel pose. Trees, ground and asphalt from Poly Haven (CC0). The far mountains and sky are an image-model painting on a curved 3D card; everything else that moves is rendered. ## Paste this to your agent [Install vork](#install), then paste: > Run `vork init my-shot`, read `vork help`, render a preview and inspect the image. > Refine the camera and lighting before rendering at final quality. Read the > relevant help topic when you need a feature the first page doesn't explain. A million birds, each steering itself over a lagoon. A black hole that bends light. A glowing seed placed on a real desk, lighting the room around it. These are scenes written as code and rendered on a GPU. No video model required. vork is written in Rust and Slang, with GPU rendering through Vulkan and Metal. An agent writes a scene, renders it, looks at the result and revises the code. There is no editor to drive. Most creative tools expose controls that a person can operate. An agent can also write a shader in the middle of a shot. vork gives it geometry, ray queries and GPU execution, then lets scene programs define materials, cameras, light propagation, simulation and compositing. Ordinary shots need only scene data; the programming hooks are there when the shot needs something unusual. Source-available and free during the research preview. ## Start here After [installing vork](#install), create a working project: ```sh vork init my-shot cd my-shot vork render scene.json --profile std/draft --out render.png vork help ``` Open `render.png`, change a colour or camera position in `scene.json`, and render again. The starter uses only bundled sphere, box and grid primitives: no downloads, no GPU needed to initialize. Use `vork init my-shot --language typescript` or `--language python` for editable `scene.ts` or `scene.py` alongside the ready-to-render JSON. The generated README explains regeneration and SDK requirements. Existing files are never overwritten. Use `--profile std/final` for a cleaner image. With the candidate npm packages (not yet published), `npm create vork my-shot` creates the same project and installs its matching native engine and TypeScript SDK from npm's cache, without network access during initialization. Then use `npx vork render scene.json --profile std/draft --out render.png` and `npx vork help` in the new directory. Pass `-- --language typescript` or `-- --language python` to select source authoring. Python source needs the Python SDK as well. ## What you can make The examples include code, preparation commands and credits. Large downloaded assets and footage stay outside Git; the recipes fetch them or accept a local path. The images here are stills from these shots. Keep each credit with its image. ### [Million birds](examples/murmuration/) | | | |---|---| | | | A million simulated agents steered by Slang compute programs, with a camera skimming through the flock. The camera and nine foreground birds are authored; the simulated million do not flap. The bird stills above come from the measured four-sample, denoised skim and reveal movies. Credit: based on ["Crow"](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/crow-d5a9b0df4da3493688b63ce42c8a83e2) by Alexei Ostapenko, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: sampled flight pose, reduced distant mesh, rescaled, articulated flight wings, extracted wings for the starling body, resized textures. [All bird and environment credits](examples/murmuration/CREDITS). ### [VFX on real footage](examples/vfx-artifact/) | Original footage | Tracked camera and proxy geometry | Final look | |---|---|---| | | | | A procedural ceramic-and-bronze seed, a tracked camera, occlusion mattes and proxy geometry for relighting. The example teaches the base composite; the final look adds later relighting and wipes. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video. Credit: footage by **Ron Lach / Pexels**, modified under the Pexels Licence. Original performer; no endorsement implied. [Source and preparation](examples/vfx-artifact/). ### [After Rain](examples/vfx-neon/) A suspended neon seed and blade sign added to a moving shot of an empty alley at night, with spill on the wall and reflections in the wet street. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video. Credit: footage is ["Ally"](https://www.pexels.com/video/ally-18972999/) by **Rafael Fernanz / Pexels**, modified under the [Pexels Licence](https://www.pexels.com/license/). [Source and preparation](examples/vfx-neon/). ### [Black hole](examples/black-hole/) The scene supplies a Schwarzschild light-propagation program through vork's public hook. Curved paths, capture and the disk's appearance live in the example. It is a numerical approximation, not an exact relativistic solver. Credit: based on ["Corinth Cargo Transporter"](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/corinth-cargo-transporter-7614d85856f6477ba2a603970dcbb0dd) by [Yvo Pors](https://sketchfab.com/yvopors14), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: decimated geometry, resized, compressed and exposure-adjusted textures, adjusted material roughness and metallic weight, placement and scale. [Ship credit](examples/black-hole/README.md#ship-credit). ### [Cake](examples/cake/) A moving camera, depth of field and daylight on detailed scanned assets. This shot is rendered 3D, using Poly Haven assets; it isn't a photographed take. Credit: Poly Haven CC0 assets; carrot cake photography by Greg Zaal, processing by James Ray Cock. [Full cake credits](examples/cake/CREDITS.md). ### [Cozy Kitchen](examples/kitchen/) Nicole Morena's Blender 3.5 splash scene, imported into vork. The recipe uses a shared material adaptation and a camera orbit; the pictured render has additional staging and animated lighting. Credit: **Cozy Kitchen** by [Nicole Morena](https://www.artstation.com/nickyblender), [source .blend](https://download.blender.org/demo/splash/blender-3.5-splash.blend), [CC BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/) (version unspecified by source). Adapted and rendered in vork: camera orbit, animated lighting, widescreen framing, material translation and staging changes. This still and the adapted animation are shared under CC BY-SA. No artist endorsement implied. [Changes and share-alike notice](examples/kitchen/CREDITS.md). ### [Water](examples/water/) A GPU liquid simulation implemented as Slang compute programs in vork's fluid library. It uses published APIC/FLIP and surface-reconstruction methods, with an authored initial impulse and limited secondary spray. ## No suitable GPU? Rendering requires Apple Silicon or an NVIDIA GPU with Vulkan ray queries. Scene authoring and `vork help` work without a GPU. On your own NVIDIA Linux machine, you can use the [Docker runtime](docs/REMOTE-GPU.md). Hosted rendering: details will be added here when available. ## Give it to an agent Start with `vork init`, then `vork help`. Scene JSON uses the stable [editor schema](https://voyager.so/vork/schema/scene.schema.json). Use `vork help` for the starting scene and concepts, `vork help TOPIC --all` for topic fields, and `vork help field PATH` for an exact field reference. Use the [prompt above](#paste-this-to-your-agent) to start. Python and TypeScript can author ordinary scene JSON through the SDKs. You can also write JSON directly. For example, save this as `scene.json` (also available as [examples/first-scene.json](examples/first-scene.json)): ```json {"version":2,"nodes":[ {"type":"mesh","geometry":{"std":"sphere","radius":1}, "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.12,0.35,0.65],"specular_roughness":0.3}}]}, {"type":"mesh","translation":[0,-1,0],"geometry":{"std":"grid","size":[10,10]}, "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.35,0.35,0.35]}}]}, {"type":"light","shape":"rectangle","translation":[-3,5,4],"target":[0,0,0], "energy":700,"size":4,"color":[1,0.92,0.8]}, {"type":"camera","translation":[3,2,5],"target":[0,0,0]} ],"render":{"resolution":[640,480]}} ``` ```sh vork render scene.json --profile std/previs --out preview.png vork render scene.json --profile std/final --out final.png vork help sdk vork help programs --all ``` Scene content and render quality are separate. Use `std/previs` to iterate, `std/draft` for scene-ray lighting at 4 samples, `std/final` for the default delivery profile, and `std/path` for path transport. Final approximates indirect lighting and can darken interiors, including glossy bounces. More samples do not restore omitted transport; try path and inspect. Draft and final use 4 and 8 samples with bundled OIDN denoising by default; use `--set denoise=false` to turn it off. `--set samples=N` overrides the profile budget (1..4096); more samples means cleaner and slower. Without a fast GPU denoiser (NVIDIA or Apple GPU), draft and final say so and use 16 and 32 samples undenoised; `--set denoise=true` runs the slow CPU denoiser anyway. For a particular field, ask `vork help field node.target`. Help topics include exact fields with `--all`. Images, video and control passes come from the same scene; see `vork help outputs`. ## Under the hood Default rendering combines raster visibility with hardware ray-traced lighting; a path tracer is also available. The scene and render plan stay installed. Frames use retained GPU resources, with GPU-to-hardware-video encoding on supported native paths. A portable encoding fallback reads pixels back to the CPU. Slang programs run on the GPU. Host parsing, planning, animation-track evaluation and IO still use the CPU. The public program hooks let a scene author change camera rays, material response, light propagation and film response without editing the renderer. `vork help programs --all` describes their scope. Validation includes furnace tests and analytic oracles, alongside render tests. That is a way to catch errors, not a guarantee that every scene is physically exact. ## Speed, with the qualifications These are timings, **not equal-quality speedups**. The draft/final results come from the build identified by SHA-256 in the results report on an NVIDIA L4: final uses eight samples and OIDN, draft four and OIDN. All 152 planned jobs were accounted for. The broader sweep delivered 583 of 585 images; the million-stars stress scene ran out of GPU memory in both profiles. Visual review found softer edges, grainier defocus, wall mottling and changed sparse or spectral highlights at these budgets. Nineteen earlier quality comparisons failed their declared no-worse FLIP condition; that experiment was not repeated for this build. vork times below are complete command wall times, including startup, scene loading, output writes and encoding. Setup, shader warmup, provisioning and transfers are excluded. Stills use five warm repetitions, movies three. Driver caches and clocks were not controlled. Blender 5.2.1 times are retained measured baselines, not fresh runs: EEVEE uses different settings, and its movie times exclude startup/loading after a still prime. Both movie timings include encoding. The car is a proxy. [Benchmark method and recorded results](benchmarks/RESULTS.md) explain the boundaries and carried-forward numbers. ### Default

releases.name: vork 0.2.0
releases.body:
# vork 0.2

## New
- `vork init` creates a working starter project in one command: JSON, TypeScript or Python.
- Setup, shader compiles and renders now show progress, instead of appearing to hang.
- When your scene asks for an effect vork can't render, it now tells you, instead of silently leaving it out.

## Better
- Re-rendering after a small code edit is much faster. A comment-only edit dropped from about 46 s to 7 s.
- Dim or high-exposure scenes no longer get crushed to near-black by the denoiser.
- Large instanced scenes (grass, crowds) set up dramatically faster.
- Many bug fixes.

## Breaking changes
Tell your agent "upgrade my scenes to vork 0.2"; the steps are in `vork help upgrade`.
- Removed: scatter builders, `renderArguments` / `render_arguments`, and the bundled `post/vignette`, `post/lens_distortion` and `post/glare` effects.
- Meshes with no material are now slightly shinier: default roughness is 0.3, previously 0.5.
- TypeScript sky and environment options now use camelCase.
- The TypeScript package is renamed from `@usevoyager/vork` to `@voyager-so/vork`.

## Known costs
- The first video after a change can take about 2 seconds longer.
- Long interior and night f

readmeHtml:
vork, the Voyager rendering kernel, is a headless 3D and VFX engine built for agents.

Watch the film: a car drives into the night as the forest turns into glowing cyan wireframe, drawn from real triangle edges by a scene shader.

Credit: “Car Concept” by Unity Fan, glTF adaptation by Eric Chadwick / Darmstadt Graphics Group, CC BY 4.0. Changes: scaled, animated, brighter head and tail lights, wheel pose. Trees, ground and asphalt from Poly Haven (CC0). The far mountains and sky are an image-model painting on a curved 3D card; everything else that moves is rendered.

Paste this to your agent

Install vork, then paste:

Run vork init my-shot, read vork help, render a preview and inspect the image. Refine the camera and lighting before rendering at final quality. Read the relevant help topic when you need a feature the first page doesn't explain.

A million birds, each steering itself over a lagoon. A black hole that bends light. A glowing seed placed on a real desk, lighting the room around it. These are scenes written as code and rendered on a GPU. No video model required.

vork is written in Rust and Slang, with GPU rendering through Vulkan and Metal. An agent writes a scene, renders it, looks at the result and revises the code. There is no editor to drive.

Most creative tools expose controls that a person can operate. An agent can also write a shader in the middle of a shot. vork gives it geometry, ray queries and GPU execution, then lets scene programs define materials, cameras, light propagation, simulation and compositing. Ordinary shots need only scene data; the programming hooks are there when the shot needs something unusual.

Source-available and free during the research preview.

Start here

After installing vork, create a working project:

vork init my-shot
cd my-shot
vork render scene.json --profile std/draft --out render.png
vork help

Open render.png, change a colour or camera position in scene.json, and render again. The starter uses only bundled sphere, box and grid primitives: no downloads, no GPU needed to initialize. Use vork init my-shot --language typescript or --language python for editable scene.ts or scene.py alongside the ready-to-render JSON. The generated README explains regeneration and SDK requirements. Existing files are never overwritten. Use --profile std/final for a cleaner image.

With the candidate npm packages (not yet published), npm create vork my-shot creates the same project and installs its matching native engine and TypeScript SDK from npm's cache, without network access during initialization. Then use npx vork render scene.json --profile std/draft --out render.png and npx vork help in the new directory. Pass -- --language typescript or -- --language python to select source authoring. Python source needs the Python SDK as well.

What you can make

The examples include code, preparation commands and credits. Large downloaded assets and footage stay outside Git; the recipes fetch them or accept a local path. The images here are stills from these shots. Keep each credit with its image.

Million birds

A million simulated agents steered by Slang compute programs, with a camera skimming through the flock. The camera and nine foreground birds are authored; the simulated million do not flap. The bird stills above come from the measured four-sample, denoised skim and reveal movies.

Credit: based on "Crow" by Alexei Ostapenko, CC BY 4.0. Changes: sampled flight pose, reduced distant mesh, rescaled, articulated flight wings, extracted wings for the starling body, resized textures. All bird and environment credits.

VFX on real footage

Original footage Tracked camera and proxy geometry Final look

A procedural ceramic-and-bronze seed, a tracked camera, occlusion mattes and proxy geometry for relighting. The example teaches the base composite; the final look adds later relighting and wipes. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video.

Credit: footage by Ron Lach / Pexels, modified under the Pexels Licence. Original performer; no endorsement implied. Source and preparation.

After Rain

A suspended neon seed and blade sign added to a moving shot of an empty alley at night, with spill on the wall and reflections in the wet street. Real footage + rendered 3D; no generative video.

Credit: footage is "Ally" by Rafael Fernanz / Pexels, modified under the Pexels Licence. Source and preparation.

Black hole

The scene supplies a Schwarzschild light-propagation program through vork's public hook. Curved paths, capture and the disk's appearance live in the example. It is a numerical approximation, not an exact relativistic solver.

Credit: based on "Corinth Cargo Transporter" by Yvo Pors, CC BY 4.0. Changes: decimated geometry, resized, compressed and exposure-adjusted textures, adjusted material roughness and metallic weight, placement and scale. Ship credit.

Cake

A moving camera, depth of field and daylight on detailed scanned assets. This shot is rendered 3D, using Poly Haven assets; it isn't a photographed take.

Credit: Poly Haven CC0 assets; carrot cake photography by Greg Zaal, processing by James Ray Cock. Full cake credits.

Cozy Kitchen

Nicole Morena's Blender 3.5 splash scene, imported into vork. The recipe uses a shared material adaptation and a camera orbit; the pictured render has additional staging and animated lighting.

Credit: Cozy Kitchen by Nicole Morena, source .blend, CC BY-SA (version unspecified by source). Adapted and rendered in vork: camera orbit, animated lighting, widescreen framing, material translation and staging changes. This still and the adapted animation are shared under CC BY-SA. No artist endorsement implied. Changes and share-alike notice.

Water

A GPU liquid simulation implemented as Slang compute programs in vork's fluid library. It uses published APIC/FLIP and surface-reconstruction methods, with an authored initial impulse and limited secondary spray.

No suitable GPU?

Rendering requires Apple Silicon or an NVIDIA GPU with Vulkan ray queries. Scene authoring and vork help work without a GPU. On your own NVIDIA Linux machine, you can use the Docker runtime. Hosted rendering: details will be added here when available.

Give it to an agent

Start with vork init, then vork help. Scene JSON uses the stable editor schema. Use vork help for the starting scene and concepts, vork help TOPIC --all for topic fields, and vork help field PATH for an exact field reference.

Use the prompt above to start.

Python and TypeScript can author ordinary scene JSON through the SDKs. You can also write JSON directly. For example, save this as scene.json (also available as examples/first-scene.json):

{"version":2,"nodes":[
  {"type":"mesh","geometry":{"std":"sphere","radius":1},
   "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.12,0.35,0.65],"specular_roughness":0.3}}]},
  {"type":"mesh","translation":[0,-1,0],"geometry":{"std":"grid","size":[10,10]},
   "materials":[{"inputs":{"base_color":[0.35,0.35,0.35]}}]},
  {"type":"light","shape":"rectangle","translation":[-3,5,4],"target":[0,0,0],
   "energy":700,"size":4,"color":[1,0.92,0.8]},
  {"type":"camera","translation":[3,2,5],"target":[0,0,0]}
],"render":{"resolution":[640,480]}}
vork render scene.json --profile std/previs --out preview.png
vork render scene.json --profile std/final --out final.png
vork help sdk
vork help programs --all

Scene content and render quality are separate. Use std/previs to iterate, std/draft for scene-ray lighting at 4 samples, std/final for the default delivery profile, and std/path for path transport. Final approximates indirect lighting and can darken interiors, including glossy bounces. More samples do not restore omitted transport; try path and inspect. Draft and final use 4 and 8 samples with bundled OIDN denoising by default; use --set denoise=false to turn it off. --set samples=N overrides the profile budget (1..4096); more samples means cleaner and slower. Without a fast GPU denoiser (NVIDIA or Apple GPU), draft and final say so and use 16 and 32 samples undenoised; --set denoise=true runs the slow CPU denoiser anyway. For a particular field, ask vork help field node.target. Help topics include exact fields with --all. Images, video and control passes come from the same scene; see vork help outputs.

Under the hood

Default rendering combines raster visibility with hardware ray-traced lighting; a path tracer is also available. The scene and render plan stay installed. Frames use retained GPU resources, with GPU-to-hardware-video encoding on supported native paths. A portable encoding fallback reads pixels back to the CPU.

Slang programs run on the GPU. Host parsing, planning, animation-track evaluation and IO still use the CPU. The public program hooks let a scene author change camera rays, material response, light propagation and film response without editing the renderer. vork help programs --all describes their scope.

Validation includes furnace tests and analytic oracles, alongside render tests. That is a way to catch errors, not a guarantee that every scene is physically exact.

Speed, with the qualifications

These are timings, not equal-quality speedups. The draft/final results come from the build identified by SHA-256 in the results report on an NVIDIA L4: final uses eight samples and OIDN, draft four and OIDN. All 152 planned jobs were accounted for. The broader sweep delivered 583 of 585 images; the million-stars stress scene ran out of GPU memory in both profiles. Visual review found softer edges, grainier defocus, wall mottling and changed sparse or spectral highlights at these budgets. Nineteen earlier quality comparisons failed their declared no-worse FLIP condition; that experiment was not repeated for this build.

vork times below are complete command wall times, including startup, scene loading, output writes and encoding. Setup, shader warmup, provisioning and transfers are excluded. Stills use five warm repetitions, movies three. Driver caches and clocks were not controlled. Blender 5.2.1 times are retained measured baselines, not fresh runs: EEVEE uses different settings, and its movie times exclude startup/loading after a still prime. Both movie timings include encoding. The car is a proxy. Benchmark method and recorded results explain the boundaries and carried-forward numbers.

Default final: stills

1080p PNG, seconds. EEVEE uses 64 samples without denoising; vork uses eight with OIDN. Missing Blender results are unmeasured, not wins.

Scene input EEVEE (s) vork final (s) Comparison
B-push-in.json 2.912 1.993 1.46× faster
B-turntable.json 3.148 2.247 1.40× faster
B-walking.json 2.612 1.890 1.38× faster
B-interior.json 2.892 1.738 1.66× faster
B-street.json unmeasured 2.043 unmeasured
B-rack-focus.json unmeasured 1.787 unmeasured
B-car-pan.json 2.458 1.691 1.45× faster
B-crowd.json unmeasured 2.046 unmeasured
B-night.json 2.963 1.937 1.53× faster

Default final: complete movies

240 frames, 1920×1080, 24 fps. These four public B-scene clips are part of the seven-scene comparison; the full seven measured 1.14–2.32× against EEVEE. Different quality and timing boundaries still apply.

Scene input EEVEE (s) vork final (s) Comparison
B-blocking.json 88.072 47.082 1.87× faster
B-interior.json 107.026 59.231 1.81× faster
B-car-pan.json 93.489 81.740 1.14× faster
B-night.json 213.477 92.201 2.32× faster

Path tracing: carried-forward measurements

These 1080p still timings were measured in an earlier build, rather than the measured final build. Adaptive sampling up to 4,096, threshold 0.01, minimum 64; stopping implementations differ. vork is slower in both cases below.

Scene input Cycles (s) vork path (s) Comparison
B-car-pan.json 4.632 26.901 5.81× slower
B-night.json 16.041 31.860 1.99× slower

Setup and first use

On B-blocking.json, the final-profile setup took 250.792 s, the first still after setup 2.298 s, and the warm median 2.094 s. The retained EEVEE cold still was 20.633 s and warm median 2.405 s. Other scenes can still spend substantial time compiling new programs after setup: rack-focus's first final still took 82.057 s, versus its 1.787 s warm median.

Previews: carried-forward measurements

These are earlier-build std/previs results, not measured on the final build identified in RESULTS.md. Previews use different lighting and shadows; these are not final-quality comparisons. Complete 240-frame, 1080p24 movies, median of three warm commands:

Scene input Preview movie (s)
B-blocking.json 3.496
B-interior.json 4.565
B-car-pan.json 6.391
B-night.json 5.864
B-crowd.json 4.097
B-push-in.json 3.705
B-rack-focus.json 3.902
B-street.json 3.964
B-turntable.json 4.612
B-walking.json 2.190

Across the seven simple preview clips on that earlier build, EEVEE/vork was 14.63–36.40× and Workbench/vork 3.99–11.24×. Those ranges use retained Blender baselines and different rendering settings and timing boundaries. They do not describe default final rendering.

Million birds: measured movies, projected Blender times

The bird inputs include the compute programs and all three cameras. These std/draft movies use four samples and OIDN at 1080p24; each number is the median of three full commands. The first full movie is included in that three-command median, after a separate 320×180 still warmup. Setup and warmup are excluded from the movie times below. For skim, setup + warmup + the movie median total 506.781 seconds (8.45 minutes); asset preparation and transfers are additional.

Camera input Frames vork movie (s) Setup (s) Warmup (s) EEVEE 16-sample projection (s), both retained runs
skim.json.in 192 96.942 243.809 166.030 1511.108 / 1817.625
dive.json.in 240 124.718 167.376 112.994 2517.891 / 2417.831
reveal.json.in 288 153.411 163.218 113.910 2916.237 / 2889.758

The EEVEE values extrapolate eight warm frames; they are projections, not measured movies. They omit simulation, startup and video encoding, and receive the finished flock as geometry. They use 16 samples against vork's four, so this table is not a like-for-like speed comparison.

The matching four-sample EEVEE projection exists only for skim: 773.7–1,082.5 s across the retained runs, with ray tracing on or off, about 8–11× the 96.9 s vork movie. Dive and reveal have no four-sample EEVEE projection. Quality, material translation and motion differ.

Rerun

python3 benchmarks/fetch.py
python3 benchmarks/run.py --vork vork --out /tmp/vork-benchmark
python3 integrations/blender/benchmark.py --blender blender --out /tmp/blender-benchmark

The vork runner measures undenoised B-scene variants, not the denoised final8 tables above. It omits draft and does not set the recorded seed 11. The bird runner uses previs/final with a full-resolution warmup, not the recorded draft4 workflow. The final8/draft4 tables use build 81ae2b075; preview and path results come from earlier freezes, as noted beside those tables.

The Blender helper currently fails during camera preparation on Blender 5.2.1. Independent reproduction of the comparisons is not working. The commands above are supplied for inspection; see the method.

Research-preview limits

Fog and participating volumes are ignored with warnings in this release. Large scenes and dense transparency can fail, including on Mac; reducing image resolution alone does not necessarily fix them. Some heavy interiors work with std/path when the default hybrid profile fails. First use of a new program can involve substantial compilation, even after vork setup.

At four/eight samples, fine facades and hair can lose detail, defocus can show stepped or grainy edges, and sparse sparks or spectral highlights can change brightness and colour. Try --set samples=32 for these shots; more samples cost more time. The frozen sweep retained a million-stars allocation failure in both profiles. Mac reliability was not revalidated in that Linux run.

The water quickstart is a closed-shutter diagnostic. The full motion-blurred scene is much more expensive. It is a uniform-grid experiment with finite particle budgets, unresolved thin features and no two-way rigid-body coupling. It is not a general replacement for a mature simulation package. The VFX camera solve and single-view relief are estimates, with limitations documented beside the example.

The next direction is fog and volumes, broader simulation, and better reliability and performance on demanding scenes. There is no release date promised for those features. Read vork help limits before committing to a shot.

Install

Upgrading scenes or scripts? Run vork help upgrade (upgrade guide).

Binary packages are available from GitHub Releases once a release is published. Keep the entire install folder together: Slang, OIDN, libraries, examples, SDKs and licence texts are runtime companions to the binary.

  • Linux: x64, glibc 2.35+ and libstdc++ with GLIBCXX_3.4.30 (Ubuntu 22.04+), a recent NVIDIA GPU and its hardware-ray-tracing Vulkan driver.
  • Windows: x64 Windows 10/11, a recent NVIDIA GPU and its hardware-ray-tracing Vulkan driver.
  • Mac: Apple Silicon with Metal, macOS 26 for the bundled Slang toolchain. Older macOS versions are unqualified. Intel Macs are unsupported. H.264 uses system VideoToolbox.

Linux

Install the NVIDIA driver for your GPU first. On Ubuntu 22.04+:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl tar libvulkan1 libgomp1 ffmpeg
curl -fL https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o /tmp/vork-install.sh
sh /tmp/vork-install.sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
vork --version
vork help

These dependency commands are for Ubuntu with sudo. In a root container, omit sudo; without administrator access, arrange for the dependencies to be installed. The installer itself runs in your user account without root.

The installer verifies SHA256SUMS, installs under $HOME/.local/lib/vork, links $HOME/.local/bin/vork, runs vork setup, and adds the PATH line to your shell's startup files, including the one login shells read. The export above covers the current shell, and any shell that reads no startup file, such as plain bash -c. VORK_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 or a custom PREFIX leaves startup files alone. Linux MP4 needs ffmpeg even when NVENC encodes frames, because ffmpeg muxes the stream. Native NVENC is attempted on NVIDIA; otherwise encoding uses a readback fallback. Older GPUs and software Vulkan adapters are unsupported. A100, H100, H200, B200 and B300 lack the required hardware ray tracing; recency alone does not make a NVIDIA GPU suitable. Containers also need working NVIDIA Vulkan driver discovery; passing through a GPU alone may not be sufficient.

Mac

The released 0.1.0 archive has these Mach-O LC_BUILD_VERSION minimums:

Binary macOS minimum
vork 11.0
slang/bin/slangc 26.0
slang/lib/libslang-compiler.0.2026.20.dylib 26.0
slang/lib/libslang-glsl-module-2026.20.dylib 26.0
oidn/lib/libOpenImageDenoise.2.5.1.dylib 11.0
oidn/lib/libOpenImageDenoise_core.2.5.1.dylib 11.0
oidn/lib/libOpenImageDenoise_device_cpu.2.5.1.dylib 11.0
oidn/lib/libOpenImageDenoise_device_metal.2.5.1.dylib 11.0
oidn/lib/libtbb.12.19.dylib 11.0

These are archive load-command targets, not tests on older macOS versions. A successful vork --version does not test Slang; new authored programs need it.

In Terminal:

curl -fL https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o /tmp/vork-install.sh
sh /tmp/vork-install.sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
vork --version
vork help

The same installer verifies and installs the complete Apple Silicon archive under $HOME/.local/lib/vork, runs setup, and adds the PATH line to your shell's startup files (.zshenv for zsh). Mac packages are signed with Apple Developer ID and notarised.

MP4 uses VideoToolbox without ffmpeg. Install ffmpeg only for video decoding or encoding fallbacks, including MOV/ProRes fallback (brew install ffmpeg).

Windows

Install the NVIDIA driver for your GPU and ffmpeg (winget install Gyan.FFmpeg). Without winget (including Windows Server 2022), download ffmpeg-release-essentials.zip from Gyan, extract it, and add its bin folder to your user PATH. Open a new PowerShell window so ffmpeg is on PATH, then:

$installer = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'vork-install.ps1'
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing https://github.com/voyager-so/vork/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 -OutFile $installer
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $installer
$env:Path = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork;$env:Path"
vork --version
vork help

The installer itself runs in your user account without root.

The installer verifies SHA256SUMS, installs under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\vork, runs vork setup, and adds that folder to your user PATH so new windows find vork; the $env:Path line above covers the current one. VORK_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 or a custom PREFIX leaves it alone. Windows MP4/MOV needs ffmpeg; MP4 uses its NVENC encoder when compatible, otherwise libx264. FFmpeg 9.0.2 requires NVENC API 13.1 (NVIDIA driver 610+) for hardware encoding; older drivers fall back to libx264. The cache is under %LOCALAPPDATA%\vork.

Manual archive install (Windows)

Download the Windows .zip and SHA256SUMS from the release page. Compare Get-FileHash .\vork-*-windows-x64.zip -Algorithm SHA256 with its entry in SHA256SUMS, then unzip the entire contents into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\vork. Add that folder to your user PATH, open a new PowerShell window, and run vork setup. It prints its report right away, then reports compilation progress until Shader setup completed. Setup can take several minutes. Keep all bundled runtime companions beside the executable.

The separately downloadable install.sh downloads the release from GitHub; to install an archive you already have without downloading again, use the manual steps below.

Manual archive install (Linux or Mac)

Download your platform's .tar.gz and SHA256SUMS from the release page into a new empty folder. In that folder, verify and install the entire archive:

set -- vork-*.tar.gz
test "$#" -eq 1 || exit 1
archive=$1
awk -v name="$archive" '$2 == name || $2 == "*" name' SHA256SUMS > selected.sha256
test "$(wc -l < selected.sha256 | tr -d ' ')" = 1 || exit 1
if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sha256sum -c selected.sha256 || exit 1
else
  shasum -a 256 -c selected.sha256 || exit 1
fi
PREFIX="$HOME/.local"
mkdir tree
tar -xzf "$archive" -C tree
mkdir -p "$PREFIX/bin" "$PREFIX/lib/vork"
cp -R tree/. "$PREFIX/lib/vork/"
ln -sf "$PREFIX/lib/vork/vork" "$PREFIX/bin/vork"
export PATH="$PREFIX/bin:$PATH"
vork --version
vork setup

vork setup prints its report right away, then reports compilation progress until Shader setup completed. Setup can take several minutes.

npm and pip installation candidate

Registry packaging is being validated privately and has not been published. Use the archive installers above and their bundled SDKs. npm and PyPI installation will become available only after separate release approval. These commands are not yet the default installation instructions.

First render and SDKs

Start with vork init my-shot and enter my-shot, then:

vork render scene.json --profile std/previs --out preview.png
vork render scene.json --profile std/final --out final.png
vork render scene.json --profile std/final --frame-start 0 --frame-end 23 --out clip.mp4
vork help animation
vork help outputs

The first render of a scene with new programs can compile for several minutes. Progress reports show shader and driver pipeline preparation; allow time for it to finish. Later renders reuse compiled programs and driver caches. Compilation time depends on the scene, GPU and cache state.

Frame ranges include both endpoints: 0 through 23 writes 24 frames. The simple scene is static; animation tracks make a moving clip. To try glTF import, save a model as model.glb beside this scene as model.json:

{"version":2,"nodes":[
  {"type":"asset","file":"model.glb"},
  {"type":"light","shape":"rectangle","translation":[-3,5,4],"target":[0,0,0],"energy":700,"size":4},
  {"type":"camera","translation":[3,2,5],"target":[0,0,0]}
],"render":{"resolution":[640,480]}}
vork render model.json --profile std/final --out model.png

Adjust the camera and light for your model's scale. glTF files can refer to textures and buffers beside them; keep those files together.

Run vork setup again after upgrading or changing GPU drivers. It prints its report right away, then reports compilation progress until Shader setup completed. Setup can take several minutes. Vulkan persists its pipeline cache when supported; Metal warms the system driver cache. New scene programs can still require compilation on their first render. VORK_CACHE_DIR overrides the cache location.

The archive includes Python 3.11+ and TypeScript SDK source/packages. Install the Python SDK into your authoring virtual environment, and the TypeScript SDK into your project (Node 22.18+ and npm):

python3 -m pip install "$HOME/.local/lib/vork/python"
npm install "$HOME/.local/lib/vork/sdk"

The SDKs install from your vork folder, not from npm or PyPI. The npm package named vork is unrelated, and the PyPI package only points back here.

On Windows use py -m pip install "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork\python" and npm install "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\vork\sdk". Import as vork in Python or @voyager-so/vork in TypeScript; keep the native executable on PATH. For source builds, see vork help build.

aiSummary.oneLiner: Distributed task queue designed for edge computing environments.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Vork is a task queue system optimized for low-latency execution across geographically distributed edge nodes. It handles task routing, ensuring jobs are executed on the node closest to the data or user. The system provides exactly-once execution guarantees and automatic retries for transient failures. It is built to operate over unreliable networks typical of edge deployments. Vork integrates with modern serverless platforms to scale worker nodes dynamically.
keyFeatures: Geographic routing: dispatches tasks to edge nodes based on proximity or data locality.
Reliable execution: guarantees exactly-once processing even during network partitions.
Dynamic scaling: automatically provisions worker nodes based on queue depth.
Priority queues: supports different priority levels to ensure critical tasks run first.
State persistence: uses distributed consensus to maintain queue state securely.
